overview: Air Liquide is the world's largest industrial gases company by revenue, producing and distributing oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, argon and specialty gases, along with related equipment and services, to industrial and healthcare customers. Founded in 1902 and headquartered in Paris, the Group serves roughly 4.3 million customers and patients across 59 countries with about 65,000 employees, generating revenue close to EUR 27 billion in 2025. The business is organized into four Gas & Services activity lines (Large Industries, Industrial Merchant, Healthcare, Electronics), reported by geography (Americas, Europe/Middle East & Africa, Asia Pacific), plus a smaller Engineering & Technologies segment that designs and builds gas production units for the Group and third parties.

business_model.summary: Air Liquide earns most of its revenue from long-term, often decades-long, contracts to supply gases to industrial and healthcare customers, with pricing mechanisms that pass through energy and inflation costs. Large Industries relies on captive on-site plants and pipeline networks under 15-20 year take-or-pay contracts; Industrial Merchant sells packaged/bulk gases to a highly diversified customer base on shorter contracts; Healthcare supplies medical gases and home care services with demand largely decoupled from the industrial cycle; and Electronics supplies ultra-pure gases, specialty materials and equipment to semiconductor and flat-panel/photovoltaic manufacturers under long-term, capital-intensive site agreements. Engineering & Technologies (merged from Engineering & Construction and Global Markets & Technologies on January 1, 2025) designs and builds production units for the Group's own capex programme and for third-party customers, generating lumpy, project-based revenue and order intake.
business_model.customer_type: Primarily B2B (industrial, chemicals, steel, refining, semiconductor manufacturers) plus Healthcare B2B2C (hospitals, home-care patients); largest customer is ~2% of revenue, top 10 ~12%, top 50 ~28% -- highly diversified
business_model.geographic_mix: FY2025 Gas & Services revenue: Europe Middle East & Africa ~41% (EUR 10,616m), Americas ~40% (EUR 10,351m), Asia Pacific ~20% (EUR 5,118m); Gas & Services is 97% of Group revenue, Engineering & Technologies 3%

main_competitors: SK Materials / regional Asian gas suppliers
competitive_position.market_position: Global #1 or #2 industrial gases producer by revenue, in a tight oligopoly: Linde, Air Liquide and Air Products together are commonly cited as controlling roughly 60-70% of the global industrial gases market, with Linde the current margin and scale leader. Air Liquide's October 2026 strategic plan and activist pressure from Elliott Management explicitly target closing an operating-margin gap versus Linde (Air Liquide ~20% operating margin vs. Linde reported closer to 30% as of mid-2026).

moat_factors.factor: Take-or-pay contracts with high switching costs
moat_factors.description: Large Industries and much of Electronics are secured by 15-20+ year take-or-pay contracts with guaranteed minimum volumes; on-site plants are built adjacent to or inside a customer's facility, making switching to a competitor prohibitively expensive and operationally disruptive.

moat_factors.factor: Local production/distribution network and asset density
moat_factors.description: Gas distribution is economic only within roughly 250km of a production site, so incumbency, pipeline networks (e.g., U.S. Gulf Coast) and a dense installed base of plants create a structural barrier to new entrants in a given industrial basin.

A small number of global players (Linde, Air Liquide, Air Products) plus a handful of regional players dominate the market, limiting price competition and supporting rational capital discipline industry-wide.
Indexed invoicing in long-term contracts transfers natural gas/electricity cost volatility to customers, protecting margins from input cost swings, though it can distort reported revenue growth.

moat_factors.factor: Technical/engineering expertise and scale in cryogenics, ASUs, electrolysis
moat_factors.description: Deep process engineering know-how (air separation, steam methane reforming, electrolysis, carbon capture) supports premium positioning in complex, first-of-a-kind decarbonization and electronics projects, though this is shared with Linde and Air Products at similar scale.
More than 4 million customers and patients across 59 countries and dozens of end markets reduce dependence on any single customer, sector or geography.

weaknesses: Operating margin trails closest peer Linde by roughly 900-1000 basis points, drawing activist (Elliott Management) criticism and creating execution pressure to deliver the new BEYOND plan
Highly capital intensive model (large multi-year industrial investments, record EUR 6.0bn backlog) exposes the Group to project execution, cost overrun and return-on-investment risk
Significant exposure to cyclical Electronics Equipment & Installation sales and to helium supply disruptions (e.g., Middle East conflict interruption in H1 2026)
Limited organic pricing power outside contracted volumes in Industrial Merchant during periods of weak industrial demand (e.g., soft 2025 in Europe/Asia Large Industries)
Complex governance structure (French double-voting-rights regime for long-term shareholders) could blunt the effectiveness of activist pressure to accelerate margin improvement

growth_drivers: Electronics/semiconductor gas demand tied to AI infrastructure build-out: record investment decisions (>EUR 1bn in H1 2026 alone, +46% vs full-year 2025) for ultra-pure gases and advanced materials supplying HBM memory, advanced packaging and chip fabs in the US, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea and China

DIG Airgas acquisition in South Korea (completed January 2026, ~EUR 3bn) roughly doubles the Group's South Korean workforce and revenue (~EUR 900m), re-establishing a leadership position in a key Electronics/semiconductor market

Hydrogen and broader decarbonization capex cycle: large-scale electrolyzer projects (e.g., 200MW ELYgator in Rotterdam), carbon capture (Cryocap, Holcim cement CCS pilot), and PPA-backed renewable power sourcing, though the sector-wide pace has slowed (termed a 'year of reckoning' by Wood Mackenzie for 2026) with industrially-anchored, contracted projects outperforming speculative ones

Healthcare structurally resilient growth from aging populations, chronic disease prevalence, Home Healthcare patient growth and higher value-added medical gas offerings (e.g., Intelli-OX, OYAN connected cylinders), largely decoupled from industrial cycles

US reshoring/onshoring of industrial and semiconductor capacity: new long-term contracts tied to steel (Hyundai-Posco Louisiana), chemicals (Gulf Coast), and chipmakers (SK hynix, other semiconductor leaders) in Indiana, Arizona, Idaho and Texas

New BEYOND 2026-2030 strategic plan targets +400 to +600bps operating margin improvement, ~5% annual revenue growth (±1pt), ~10% annual recurring EPS growth (±2pts), >11% ROCE by 2030, and an unprecedented EUR 4bn share buyback alongside >EUR 40bn of total capital allocation
Space, quantum computing and deep-tech niches (Ariane 6, ITER, superconducting cables, Quobly quantum investment) provide small but high-technology-content growth optionality

business.description: Cryogenic, high-pressure and high-temperature processes across thousands of local production and distribution sites carry burn, fire, explosion and transportation accident risk.

Record investment backlog (EUR 6.0bn, >70 projects) and investment decisions (EUR 2.9bn in H1 2026 alone) expose the Group to design, construction, cost-overrun and project-profitability risk, especially in first-of-a-kind decarbonization technologies (electrolyzers, carbon capture, ammonia cracking).

While aggregate customer concentration is low (top customer ~2% of revenue), individual on-site plants are often built for a single customer, so that customer's bankruptcy, closure or demand collapse can strand an asset.

business.risk: Helium and specialty molecule supply concentration
business.description: Helium and certain rare gases are produced at a limited number of sites worldwide; disruptions (e.g., the Middle East conflict interrupting a helium source in H1 2026) directly hit Industrial Merchant volumes and margins.

Equipment & Installation sales within Electronics are more cyclical than Carrier Gases/Advanced Materials and have normalized downward after record 2024 levels; semiconductor capex cycles can create volatile period-over-period comparisons.

financial.risk: Rising net debt and leverage from M&A
financial.description: Net debt rose to EUR 13.9bn at June 30, 2026 (from EUR 9.8bn a year earlier), with net debt/equity (dividend-seasonality adjusted) climbing to 45.1% from 31.2% at YE2025, driven by the ~EUR 3bn DIG Airgas acquisition, dividends and industrial capex.

Reporting in euros while generating significant revenue in USD and other currencies creates translation risk; a negative currency impact of -3.6% to -3.7% reduced H1 2026 published growth, and dollar depreciation accounted for roughly half of a -3.2% FY2025 currency drag.

Cost of net debt rose given new DIG Airgas financing (+27.4% in H1 2026), though average cost of net debt actually declined to 3.0% from 3.3%; counterparty risk is managed conservatively via investment-grade banks only.
Effective tax rate rose to 26.4% in H1 2026 from 25.1%, partly due to non-deductibility of DIG Airgas acquisition costs and an exceptional tax surcharge in France.

regulatory.risk: Carbon pricing / emissions trading scheme changes
regulatory.description: EU ETS and other carbon-pricing regimes affect production costs; declining free allowances could require compensatory measures, though long-term contracts generally pass CO2 costs to customers.
Medical devices, drug and patient-data regulations create compliance costs and risk of non-compliance penalties across the Healthcare business line.

Exposure to sanctions regimes (notably Russia, where operations have been deconsolidated since September 2022 and a Provisional Administrator decree was issued in August 2025) and broader trade-compliance obligations.

Changes in public hydrogen/decarbonization mandates (e.g., potential EU rollback of industrial hydrogen targets flagged by analysts for 2026) could slow the pace or economics of the Group's energy-transition investment pipeline.

macro.description: Management explicitly cited 'significant geopolitical instability leading to reduced visibility' in its H1 2026 outlook; the Middle East conflict has already disrupted helium supply and affected refinery/chemical customer demand patterns.

macro.risk: Industrial demand cyclicality in Europe and parts of Asia
macro.description: Weak Large Industries and Industrial Merchant demand in Europe (notably cogeneration/steam in Benelux) and parts of Asia (Singapore, China ex-Electronics) has weighed on segment growth even as Americas and Electronics outperform.

Natural gas and electricity price swings are largely passed through contractually, but the 'energy impact' adjustment itself introduces reported-vs-comparable revenue divergence that can confuse headline growth figures.

Industry-wide, large speculative clean-hydrogen projects are being delayed or cancelled (e.g., peer Air Products' Louisiana project), even as industrially-anchored, contracted projects proceed; a broader pullback would affect Air Liquide's energy-transition investment backlog and return expectations.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global industrial gases market is a mature, consolidated oligopoly (Linde, Air Liquide, Air Products controlling an estimated 60-70% of a market sized roughly $120bn) growing mid-single-digits annually, with above-average growth pockets in Electronics/semiconductor gases (driven by AI-related chip demand) and decarbonization-linked large industrial projects; clean hydrogen specifically faces a more cautious 2026-2027 after 2025's project cancellations and delays industry-wide.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate and well-diversified: Large Industries and Industrial Merchant track industrial production cycles (currently soft in Europe/parts of Asia, resilient in the Americas), Electronics tracks semiconductor capex cycles (currently strong on AI-driven demand), while Healthcare is largely non-cyclical/defensive.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate -- the Group carries meaningful net debt (EUR 13.9bn at June 2026) that is growing with M&A and capex, financed through bond issuance (e.g., CHF640m EMTN issue in H1 2026 at <1% weighted average rate); higher rates raise financing costs for its large, multi-year investment backlog.

recent_developments.event: Completed the ~EUR 3 billion acquisition of DIG Airgas in South Korea (ahead of schedule), roughly doubling the Group's South Korean workforce and adding ~EUR 900m of revenue; its largest acquisition since Airgas in 2016.

Activist investor Elliott Investment Management disclosed it had built a stake in Air Liquide and is pushing management to close the operating-margin gap with Linde (Air Liquide ~21% vs. Linde ~30% as of mid-2026 per LSEG data); shares rose several percent on the news.

H1 2026 results: revenue EUR 13,828m (+4.3% ex-currency/energy, +2.6% comparable), Operating Income Recurring EUR 2,893m (+5.7% published, margin 20.9%, +110bps ex-energy/PPA), net profit (Group share) EUR 1,823m (+1.2%); net debt rose to EUR 13.9bn on DIG Airgas financing, dividends and capex; record H1 investment decisions of EUR 2.9bn (+27%) and record investment backlog of EUR 6.0bn.

Hosted Capital Markets Day and unveiled the 'BEYOND' strategic plan for 2026-2030: targets +400 to +600bps cumulative operating margin improvement, ~5% annual revenue growth (±1pt), ~10% annual recurring EPS growth (±2pts), >11% recurring ROCE by 2030, more than EUR 40bn of total capital allocation, and the Group's first-ever large-scale share buyback (EUR 4bn). Elliott Management publicly welcomed the plan.
Divested biogas production activities in the United States, France, Norway and Sweden, and certain Healthcare businesses in France and Switzerland, as part of ongoing portfolio optimization.

Record Electronics investment momentum: more than EUR 1bn of Electronics investment decisions in H1 2026 alone (+46% vs. full-year 2025), tied to AI/semiconductor demand (SK hynix HBM memory packaging in the US and South Korea, new Japan and Singapore fabs, Taiwan Advanced Materials plant).

Completed the merger of Engineering & Construction and Global Markets & Technologies into a single 'Engineering & Technologies' business unit (effective January 1, 2025), with Biomethane and Maritime activities transferred to Industrial Merchant.

guidance.as_of: H1 2026 results (July 2026) and Capital Markets Day (October 5, 2026)
guidance.fiscal_year: FY2026 and BEYOND plan through FY2030

items.notes: Confirms prior objective; part of a cumulative +560bps ambition over 2022-2027 (+100bps FY2026 plus a newly introduced +100bps FY2027 objective announced in February 2026).
No specific percentage given; qualitative confidence reaffirmed in H1 2026 report amid 'significant geopolitical instability leading to reduced visibility.'

items.target: Similar to or slightly higher than H1 2026 growth
items.notes: Qualitative guidance given with H1 2026 results, citing both potential upsides and geopolitical instability.

items.target: +400 to +600 basis points, excluding energy impact
items.notes: Announced at the October 5, 2026 Capital Markets Day; explicitly aimed at closing the margin gap versus Linde; welcomed by activist investor Elliott Management.
Part of the BEYOND plan long-term financial framework.
Part of the BEYOND plan; combines margin expansion, moderate growth and the new buyback's EPS accretion.
H1 2026 recurring ROCE already stood at 11.0%, stable year-on-year despite dilution from accelerating investment-under-construction.
More than half earmarked for industrial investment plus bolt-on and strategic M&A; the remainder funds the new buyback and dividends.

items.target: EUR 1,828m in H1 2026 (annualizing toward a multi-year elevated run rate)
items.notes: Industrial capex was roughly flat H1 2026 vs H1 2025 (EUR 1,828m vs EUR 1,836m), while total capex (including the DIG Airgas acquisition) reached EUR 4,956m.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO François Jackow and Chairman Benoît Potier both emphasized 2025 as a 'record performance' year and described the operating environment for 2026 as one of 'moderate growth' amid reshoring, AI-driven demand, and energy transition megatrends. The H1 2026 outlook statement explicitly flagged 'significant geopolitical instability leading to reduced visibility' while reaffirming confidence in margin and recurring net profit targets. The BEYOND plan announcement (October 5, 2026) was explicitly positioned as a response to investor calls (including Elliott Management) for faster margin convergence toward Linde's level and more active capital returns via the Group's first major buyback.

bull_case: Oligopoly industry structure with long-dated take-or-pay contracts and on-site plants provides exceptional revenue visibility, high switching costs and resilient cash flow across economic cycles

New BEYOND 2026-2030 plan, catalyzed by activist investor Elliott Management, sets credible, quantified targets (+400-600bps margin improvement, ~10% EPS CAGR, first-ever EUR 4bn buyback) that could substantially re-rate the stock if delivered, especially versus the margin-leading peer Linde

Electronics/semiconductor gas demand is a genuine secular growth engine tied to AI infrastructure buildout, with record investment decisions, a reinforced South Korean platform via DIG Airgas, and leadership positions in Taiwan, Japan and the US
Healthcare and Industrial Merchant provide non-cyclical/diversified ballast, while US reshoring and Gulf Coast pipeline demand support Large Industries growth even as Europe stays soft
Energy and inflation cost pass-through mechanisms in long-term contracts structurally protect margins from commodity price volatility, a rare feature versus most industrial peers
bear_case: Persistent operating-margin gap versus Linde (roughly 900-1000bps as of mid-2026) raises the question of whether Air Liquide's business mix, governance (French double-voting-rights structure) or execution can really close the gap, or whether the BEYOND targets prove overly ambitious

Rising leverage from the DIG Airgas acquisition (net debt up to EUR 13.9bn, net debt/equity to 45.1%) combined with a new EUR 4bn buyback commitment could strain the balance sheet if industrial demand in Europe/Asia stays weak or capex needs increase further

Clean hydrogen and broader decarbonization capex cycle is entering a more cautious phase industry-wide (termed a 'year of reckoning' for 2026), creating risk that large energy-transition investments in the backlog are delayed, rescoped or deliver lower returns than planned

Heavy reliance on a small number of mega-projects and long investment-decision-to-start-up lead times (years) means near-term results depend on execution of a large, complex and growing project backlog (EUR 6.0bn, >70 projects) with inherent cost-overrun and delay risk

Geopolitical instability (Middle East conflict disrupting helium supply, Russia exposure, broader macro uncertainty) explicitly cited by management as reducing visibility into H2 2026 and beyond, and currency headwinds (dollar weakness) continue to dampen published growth and profit figures
